subject: Shore Based Counts Using ONLY ONE LINE TRANSECT

messages.author: 5b9bd08015dd7594
messages.subject: Shore Based Counts Using ONLY ONE LINE TRANSECT
parts:
Hello Everyone,

I am a masters student course work student and new to distance sampling. I
am undertaking a small research project involving the use of distance
sampling from a shore based platform to estimate daily densities of
migratory humpback whales.

Having read applicable sections of the Distance text in relation to
line transects and other articles regarding measurements of distance from
shore for migratory whales, I find that I still need some clarification on
several points as to obtaining distance measurements with respect using
line transects.

Since the whales will be passing a stationary point (coming from the same
direction) is it more appropriate to use a =93one-sided=94 line transect in
which the width is undefined for the one side of the transect? Then take
distance measurements as the whale groups approach some pre-defined
centreline (maybe defined by a degree measurement)? (Survey area would be
defined by the field of view from initial detection southernmost point to
the centreline)

Other articles I have read in relation to distance measurements and shore
based counts only describe that measurements were taken when whale groups
were approximately in line with the counting station. However, it is
unclear what is meant by =93approximate=94 or how this width of the transect=

from a centreline was defined.

Would it be more appropriate to define widths on either side of the
centreline of the line transect to collect distance data? Only doing this
would cause the widths to be extremely wide and that does not appear to be
correct.

Thank you in advance for assistance.

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Shore Based Counts Using ONLY ONE LINE TRANSECT
parts:
Lisa, line transect methods are inappropriate for land-based surveys of
humpback whales. The animals are not uniformly distributed with respect
to distance from the shore. Put another way, you don't have a large
number of lines, positioned randomly with respect to the whales. Take a
look at the section on 'migration counts' in the 1993 distance sampling
book (which is on the RUWPA web page - see below).

Steve Buckland
